query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, well‐controlled amount of interstitial oxygen into a high‐entropy alloy (HEA) can improve its magnetocaloric effect by increasing lattice distortions that alter magnetic exchange interactions.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic, single-phase high‐entropy alloy with a random solid solution structure (for example, a Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti system) without significant interstitial doping.
generation.intervention: Incorporate controlled interstitial oxygen during alloy processing (e.g., during sintering or deposition) so that oxygen is dissolved uniformly without forming large oxide precipitates.
generation.conditions: High-temperature processing under a controlled atmosphere to ensure uniform oxygen uptake and retention in the interstitial sites, with subsequent cooling and minimal secondary phase formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased lattice distortion and modified local chemical environments caused by interstitial oxygen atoms.
generation.mechanism: The oxygen atoms, located in interstitial sites, cause local lattice strain and subtle changes to electronic environments. These modifications can adjust the magnetic exchange interactions in the alloy, leading to a potentially higher magnetic entropy change (ΔSm) when an external magnetic field is applied.
generation.predicted_outcome: When measured with magnetocaloric characterization (e.g., isothermal magnetization studies), the oxygen-doped HEA is expected to exhibit an increased magnetic entropy change and improved cooling capacity compared to the oxygen-free counterpart.
generation.baseline: The undoped HEA with a standard magnetocaloric response that serves as the reference.
generation.boundary: There is a narrow window of oxygen concentration where beneficial lattice distortion occurs; excessive oxygen may result in oxide precipitation and degradation of magnetic (and mechanical) properties.
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence linking interstitial oxygen addition in HEAs to improved magnetocaloric properties is limited. The hypothesis is extrapolated from observed effects of interstitial elements on other functional properties (e.g., mechanical relaxation processes) in HEAs, and further experimental validation is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of an equiatomic Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti HEA: one set processed with controlled oxygen doping and one set processed under oxygen‐free conditions. Characterize both the microstructural changes (using XRD and TEM) and the magnetocaloric effect via isothermal magnetization measurements across a range of temperatures.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns to verify phase purity and detect lattice distortion
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe local structure and confirm oxygen distribution
Magnetization measurements (using a vibrating sample magnetometer or PPMS) to evaluate the magnetic entropy change (ΔSm) under applied fields
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped HEA does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in magnetic entropy change compared to the undoped HEA under identical processing conditions, or if secondary oxide phases form leading to degraded magnetic performance, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. We observed that the relaxation peaks in the current HEAs are asymmetrically broadened (see Fig. 1, A to C ). This is a feature associated with the variety of interstitial relaxation processes involved in these massive solid solutions ( [28] ). Because of the complexity in alloy composition and the resulting multitude in local chemical environments in which the interstitial atoms switch their positions, it is difficult to conduct a complete peak deconvolution analysis based on all possible individual relaxation processes. However, two main configurations of the interstitial atoms can indeed be distinguished in the current material, namely, position switches of interstitials in ordered interstitial complexes and relaxation of randomly distributed interstitial atoms ( [22] ). These two kinds of configurations both contribute to the current Snoek relaxation and can cause at least some of the asymmetries observed. Therefore, we conduct a decomposition of the relaxation structure in terms of the two main classes of interstitial configurations (see the Supplementary Materials).
